patient.chief_complaint: Recurrent stereotyped spells with déjà vu, right-hand automatisms, and brief unresponsiveness
patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. Sharma is a 26-year-old left-handed South Asian graduate engineering student who presents to the inpatient neurology service after a witnessed spell at his university library. A fellow student reports that he suddenly stopped reading, stared straight ahead, and began making repetitive fumbling movements with his right hand as if sorting through pages. He was unresponsive to his name for approximately 50 to 70 seconds. Afterward, he appeared confused and asked where he was; he oriented fully within five minutes but reported feeling fatigued and had no memory of the event.

On further questioning, Mr. Sharma describes a pattern of recurrent episodes over the past 11 months. Each spell begins with a sudden, intensely vivid sense of familiarity — he knows an event has not actually happened before, but cannot shake the feeling — accompanied by a rising warmth in his chest and a brief sensation of fear. He usually remains aware during the initial phase but sometimes notices a gap in memory immediately following. He estimates these events occur approximately once or twice per month, though several witnesses have told him he performs brief repetitive right-hand movements during the episodes. He reports two to three occasions of waking with a feeling of exhaustion and mild tongue soreness without clear memory of nocturnal activity, raising concern for unwitnessed nocturnal events.

He sought medical attention approximately 14 months ago for headaches and underwent a standard brain MRI at an outside facility, which was reported as showing no acute abnormality. That report was used to reassure him that his spells were not seizure-related and were attributed to stress. He has not had prior EEG. He denies any head trauma, CNS infection, or new medications. He takes no recreational drugs and has not had alcohol within the past 48 hours.

mri.impression: 1. Subtle focal cortical thickening with blurred grey-white junction and transmantle FLAIR signal in the posterior left superior temporal gyrus, measuring approximately 2.0 x 1.5 cm on the most involved coronal slice. This finding was not identified on the prior standard brain MRI (5 mm axial sequences); it is demonstrated on the current dedicated epilepsy-protocol study using 2 mm thin coronal sequences and 3D-T1. Imaging features are most consistent with a focal cortical dysplasia. Low-grade neoplasm (DNET, ganglioglioma) cannot be excluded on imaging alone; absence of enhancement argues against higher-grade lesion. 2. Symmetric, normal hippocampal volumes bilaterally. results.title: Detection of focal cortical dysplasia on standard versus epilepsy-protocol MRI: systematic review
results.summary: Standard clinical MRI (5 mm axial sequences) misses FCD in 20-40% of cases that are identified on dedicated epilepsy-protocol MRI (1-2 mm thin coronal cuts through the temporal lobes, 3D-T1, FLAIR). FCD is characterized by cortical thickening, blurring of the grey-white junction, and transmantle FLAIR sign (T-sign). High-resolution 3T epilepsy-protocol MRI is recommended for all patients with suspected focal epilepsy.

results.title: Focal cortical dysplasia: ILAE classification and clinical spectrum
results.summary: FCD is classified by histopathological type (I: laminar disorganization; II: dysmorphic neurons +/- balloon cells; III: associated with another lesion). FCD Type IIb (balloon cells) most commonly shows the transmantle sign on MRI. Temporal lobe FCD may present with complex focal-onset seizures at any age.

results.title: AED selection for structural focal epilepsy: ILAE evidence-based guideline
results.summary: Carbamazepine, lacosamide, lamotrigine, levetiracetam, and oxcarbazepine are supported for focal-onset seizures. Structural etiology (FCD, hippocampal sclerosis, low-grade tumor) does not differentially favor one AED over others for seizure control. Early AED introduction is appropriate after a second unprovoked seizure.

output.summary: Focal cortical dysplasia is a leading cause of drug-resistant focal epilepsy and is frequently missed on standard brain MRI. Dedicated epilepsy-protocol MRI with thin coronal cuts, 3D-T1, and optimized FLAIR sequences identifies FCD in a significant proportion of cases initially reported as normal on standard imaging. Key MRI features include cortical thickening, blurred grey-white junction, and the transmantle sign. First-line AED options for structural focal epilepsy include levetiracetam, lamotrigine, carbamazepine, and lacosamide.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Focal epilepsy of left temporal lobe origin (focal cortical dysplasia)

differential.diagnosis: MRI-negative focal epilepsy of left temporal lobe origin
differential.key_features: Prior standard MRI reported as normal creates anchoring toward MRI-negative epilepsy; overcome by recognizing the inadequacy of the standard protocol and ordering epilepsy-protocol MRI.
Left temporal EEG focus and déjà vu aura raise hippocampal sclerosis; hippocampal volumes are symmetric and normal, making this less likely than neocortical FCD.
Focal cortical lesion in a young patient without enhancement; imaging features (grey-white blurring, transmantle sign) favor FCD over DNET/ganglioglioma, but histological confirmation needed.

differential.diagnosis: Extratemporal focal epilepsy (frontal or parietal lobe origin)
differential.key_features: Left anterior temporal EEG phase reversal (F7/T3) and consistent temporal semiology argue against extratemporal origin; no frontal or parietal imaging abnormality.
Stereotyped semiology, right-hand automatisms, post-ictal confusion, and elevated prolactin argue against pure PNES; video-EEG captures electrographic ictal correlate.

Interictal exam typically normal; subtle verbal memory deficit may be elicited.

useless_tools.rationale: No clinical features of CNS infection, encephalitis, or immunocompromise; CSF analysis is not indicated for routine focal epilepsy workup.
Semiology is clearly seizure-like; convulsive syncope is not on the differential once EEG and MRI findings are obtained; ECG adds no diagnostic value here.
No syncope-versus-seizure question; no structural cardiac concern; echocardiogram contributes nothing to focal epilepsy workup.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is reserved for syncope-versus-seizure differentiation; not indicated when EEG confirms epileptiform focus.
Non-contrast head CT cannot detect focal cortical dysplasia or subtle cortical lesions; inferior to MRI for epilepsy localization and adds ionizing radiation without diagnostic yield.

sequence_constraints.reason: Structural cause (FCD versus low-grade tumor versus hippocampal sclerosis) influences AED choice and counseling regarding surgical candidacy; MRI result should precede definitive drug selection.

critical_actions: Do not accept a normal standard brain MRI as excluding a structural epileptogenic lesion — order a dedicated epilepsy-protocol MRI (thin coronal cuts, 3D-T1, FLAIR) when EEG localizes a temporal focus.
Recognize the teaching point: the prior standard MRI (5 mm axial sequences) failed to detect an FCD visible only on 2 mm thin epilepsy-protocol coronal sequences.
Initiate an appropriate first-line AED for structural focal epilepsy (levetiracetam, lamotrigine, lacosamide, or oxcarbazepine) after MRI and drug interaction review.
Refer to a comprehensive epilepsy center for surgical evaluation given identified FCD concordant with EEG lateralization — FCD is a potentially curable cause of focal epilepsy.
Counsel on driving restrictions per locally applicable seizure-free interval regulations.
contraindicated_actions: Do not label this patient as MRI-negative on the basis of the outside standard brain MRI alone; a prior normal standard MRI does not exclude FCD.
Do not perform lumbar puncture; no indication for CSF analysis in this presentation.
Do not order a non-contrast head CT as a substitute for MRI in the epilepsy evaluation.
Do not dismiss the lesion as a benign incidental finding; left temporal EEG concordance with the MRI abnormality requires clinical integration.
key_reasoning_points: FCD is frequently invisible on standard brain MRI (5 mm axial sequences) but detectable on epilepsy-protocol MRI with thin coronal cuts through the temporal lobes and 3D-T1 sequences; a prior normal standard MRI should never be used to rule out a structural lesion when EEG localizes a temporal focus.

The MRI signature of FCD — focal cortical thickening, blurred grey-white junction, and transmantle FLAIR sign — requires dedicated thin-cut coronal imaging; these features are absent or undetectable on standard clinical brain MRI.

EEG-MRI concordance is essential: the left anterior temporal EEG focus (F7/T3 phase reversal) and the left posterior superior temporal gyrus FCD are anatomically concordant, strengthening the epileptogenic localization.
Semiology in left temporal epilepsy characteristically includes right-hand automatisms (contralateral to the dominant hemisphere lesion), which are lateralizing and must be recognized as such.
FCD of the temporal lobe is potentially surgically remediable; early referral to a comprehensive epilepsy center is appropriate after establishing concordance between EEG and MRI.

red_herrings.data_point: Standard brain MRI performed 14 months prior reported as 'no acute intracranial abnormality' — standard protocol without epilepsy-protocol thin coronal sequences.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on the normal prior MRI and conclude that structural MRI-negative focal epilepsy is the most likely diagnosis, missing the FCD that is only visible on epilepsy-protocol sequences.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A standard brain MRI cannot exclude focal cortical dysplasia; the epilepsy-protocol MRI (thin coronal cuts, 3D-T1, FLAIR) is the appropriate imaging for patients with focal EEG abnormalities, and it reveals the left posterior temporal FCD not seen on the prior standard study.
